scope: The scored batch's rust-errors, go-page and go-relationships fixtures, Git and Falinks arms (#228 decision 4); and #205's go-invoice in its three arms, one agent, two Git agents and two Falinks agents (#336). A team of one's final snapshot is measured as a two-agent team's: the same metrics, properties and ratings.

amendments.reason: None of the three references has test code, so a happy-path-only test copy would add tests to a test-free reference and could not rate lower on test_quality. The known-answer base is therefore the reference plus thorough tests, and every copy degrades that base (Daniel, 2026-10-23, on #233). unnecessary_changes also admits an added declaration nobody asked for: go-page and go-relationships each have only declarations the requirements name, so their copies add one instead of rewriting one; rust-errors names every declaration too, so its copy adds one as well. judge.calibration_record names where the record goes, versioned so an amendment never overwrites it.

Calibration on manifest v31 (calibration/v2.json): every dimension's copy rated lower than the reference on all three fixtures, so all four dimensions passed on the first calibration and none was amended or dropped. judge.calibration records the outcome the report reads.

Fixture 3 version 2 (#139, landed by #250), before any value was computed. L3 now checks Parse and IDs and L4 checks Stats and Duplicates, keeping 13 properties. Leading zeros are decided by the requirement (an id written with ASCII digits only, positive): 007 parses as 7 and 000 is rejected; L3's domain adds both ids and states that its other half is an id, ':' and an L1 line, longer than 20. L4's domain draws words from a, b and ab so texts repeat, and its broken copy changes Duplicates. L3 and L4 quote every sentence they compare. Judge material (decision 16): file names are removed from the code; the requirement text is shown verbatim, file names included, because it is the same for both arms. The calibration on manifest v31 (calibration/v2.json) used a known-answer set built on fixture 3 version 1, so go-relationships is listed in uncalibrated_fixtures: its judge cells print Not yet calibrated, and the inspection rule stays in force for it, until a follow-up recalibrates it on a new known-answer set (Daniel, 2026-10-23, on #250).

Recalibration of go-relationships on fixture 3 version 2 (#263). Its known-answer set was rebuilt on the v2 reference: records_test.go covers Produce, Consume, Stats, Duplicates, Parse and IDs, and the four copies (Daniel signed them off) were frozen in manifest v35 before any calibration call. Decision 23 is read as allowing a new set for a new fixture version: no calibrated copy changed. Only go-relationships was rated (calibration/v4.json, 15 calls); rust-errors and go-page keep calibration/v2.json, because nothing the judge reads for them (fixture, reference, copies, prompt, anchors, material code, runtime pin) changed since it. duplication, test_quality and unnecessary_changes passed (reference medians 5, 4 and 5; copy medians 2, 1 and 3). maintainability tied at median 4 (reference 4,4,5; copy 4,4,3): every copy reason named its manual loop, but the reference lost a point for Duplicates' count reset. maintainability is dropped for go-relationships only, where it prints Failed calibration; not reported. It stays calibrated on rust-errors and go-page, whose reported values are unchanged, and its prompt is not amended (Daniel, 2026-10-24, on #263). go-relationships leaves uncalibrated_fixtures, and the inspection rule is lifted for it.

#205's code quality (#205 resolution, "Code quality"): go-invoice and the one-agent arm join the scope. Properties I1-I9 add one per ticket, 22 in all; the reference passes them and each fails on its broken copy. None calls discount.Line, whose result the requirement leaves to the implementer (#332): I3 reads each rule's discount through Totals with a zero tax Table, as the oracle does, and a reference variant with the other choice passes all nine. The suite prints only what the requirements fix; the new exclusions name what it leaves out. Titles are never empty, since whether a rule drops the trailing spaces of an empty last column is open; an error's Line is the first bad line, the one a line-by-line reader meets. The known-answer base is the reference plus invoice_test.go, one test function with a subtest per ticket, so the test_quality copy changes one declaration; it checks errors by type assertion, so the copy leaves no import unused. The copies: Statement sums the discount, tax and total itself instead of calling Totals (duplication); an unrequested render.Markdown (unnecessary_changes); Validate as a flag-driven loop (maintainability); happy-path tests (test_quality). Daniel signs off each copy as plausible (subtlety_rule). This version freezes the copies for that review; a copy he changes is re-frozen in a new version before the first calibration call, and none changes after it (amendment_rule). go-invoice is in uncalibrated_fixtures, so its judge cells print Not yet calibrated until `known-answer --judge CONFIG --fixtures go-invoice` (15 calls) records its calibration and a further amendment sets each dimension's outcome; a dimension that fails is dropped for go-invoice alone (#263). The blinding question assumes two agents, so a team of one is rated but not asked it. No go-invoice run exists and its scored batch (#339) follows its calibration, so the lifted inspection rule needs no exception.

Calibration of go-invoice (calibration/v6.json, 15 calls), run by Daniel outside auto mode on the copies as frozen in v6, none changed. The record names manifest v46, this branch's freeze before it was rebased onto #364, which took v46 first; v47 holds the same files except config.json's protocol text, which the judge does not read. Only go-invoice was rated; rust-errors, go-page and go-relationships keep their records, because nothing the judge reads for them changed. All four dimensions passed on the first calibration (reference medians 3, 4, 4 and 4; copy medians 2, 3, 1 and 2 for duplication, maintainability, test_quality and unnecessary_changes), so none is amended or dropped. judge.calibration records go-invoice's outcome, and go-invoice leaves uncalibrated_fixtures.

The Claude Code pin moves from 2.1.308 to 2.1.309 (#382), before #205's final freeze (#338) and before any #205 value was computed. falinks-arm requires the run configuration's runtime_version to equal the adapter's pin, and the judge requires judge.runtime_version to equal the run configuration's, so the judge pin moves with them (Daniel, 2026-10-31, on #382). The judge model, prompt, anchors, k, material and rules are unchanged. The calibration records stand and were not re-run: calibration/v2.json, v4.json and v6.json were made on 2.1.308, and only the CLI version the calls go through changed.

Step A's fixture library-loans (#498) gets its protected properties L1-L9, one per ticket in go-invoice's style, with one broken copy each in protected/properties/broken.json. They use the frozen seed and input count. T2's DaysBetween is read as the trap's correction fixes it (both ends counted), as the oracle reads it. library-loans is not a judged fixture, so no calibration record or judge setting changes; the other fixtures' properties are unchanged.

list.checks: ParseMoney and ParseRate values and errors, Money and Rate String and their round trips, MulRate's and DivRound's rounding, and DivRound's panic on 0

requirement.text: Money is an amount in cents (int64). ParseMoney(s string) (Money, error) accepts an optional leading -, one or more ASCII digits, and optionally a . followed by one or two digits; it returns an error for anything else, including spaces, a leading + and amounts outside int64. "-0" is 0. String() prints a - for a negative amount, the whole units in decimal without leading zeros (0 below one unit), a . and exactly two digits, so ParseMoney(m.String()) is m. Rate is a nonnegative factor in millionths (int64): 1000000 is 1 and 82500 is 8.25%. ParseRate(s string) (Rate, error) accepts one or more digits, optionally followed by a . and one to six digits, or the same with at most four decimals followed directly by %, which divides it by 100; it returns an error for anything else, including a sign, spaces and values outside int64. Rate's String() formats it as a percentage with at most four decimals, dropping trailing zeros and a trailing ., followed by %, such as 8.25%, 100% or 0%, so ParseRate(r.String()) is r. (m Money) MulRate(r Rate) Money returns m × r ÷ 1,000,000 rounded to the nearest cent, halves away from zero, exactly whenever m × r fits in int64. DivRound(a, b int64) int64 returns a ÷ b rounded to the nearest integer, halves away from zero, and panics when b is 0.

list.domain: amounts as an optional -, 1-6 digits and an optional . with 0-3 digits, rates likewise with 0-7 decimals or as percentages with 0-5, strings of 0-8 characters from digits, '-', '.', '+', '%', 'e' and space, and edge strings at the int64 limits; any int64 Money and nonnegative Rate printed and parsed back; MulRate on amounts up to ±10^9 cents and rates up to 3, halves included; DivRound on numerators up to ±10^12 and divisors -20 to 20, 0 included
excluded: error messages
the value returned with an error

list.checks: Gross, Subtotal, Validate's first broken rule and its Line, and Summarize

requirement.text: LineItem{SKU string; Qty int64; Unit Money; Category string} is Qty units of SKU at Unit each, and its Gross() is Qty × Unit. Invoice{ID, Customer, Currency string; Lines []LineItem} has Subtotal(), the sum of its lines' Gross. Validate() error returns nil for a valid invoice, or an *Error for the first rule it breaks, checked in this order: ID is nonempty and has no whitespace; Customer is not empty or only whitespace; Currency is three ASCII capital letters; there is at least one line; then, line by line, SKU is nonempty, has no whitespace and is not used by an earlier line, Qty is at least 1, Unit is not negative, and Category is nonempty and made only of ASCII lowercase letters, digits and -. Error.Line is the 1-based index of the line at fault, or 0 for the invoice's own fields, including having no lines; Msg is free text. In the root package invoice, Summary starts with ID, Customer string and Subtotal core.Money, and Summarize(inv core.Invoice) Summary returns inv's ID, Customer and Subtotal with every other field zero.

list.checks: ParseRules values, error lines and nil slice, Rule.String, and the discount each rule set takes, read through Totals with a zero tax Table

requirement.text: ParseRules(text string) ([]Rule, error) reads one rule per line of text, split at \n. Spaces, tabs and \r are trimmed from both ends of each line, blank lines and lines starting with # are skipped, and fields are separated by whitespace. A rule is one of: percent CATEGORY RATE [min QTY] [cap AMOUNT], which takes RATE of the Gross off each line in CATEGORY with at least QTY units (QTY defaults to 1); tier CATEGORY QTY:RATE... [cap AMOUNT], one or more tiers with strictly increasing quantities, which takes off each line in CATEGORY the RATE of its Gross of the last tier whose QTY the line's Qty reaches, and nothing below the first; bundle SKU BUY FREE, which takes Qty ÷ (BUY + FREE), rounded down, × FREE × Unit off the line with that SKU; and off SKU AMOUNT, which takes AMOUNT, but at most Unit, off each unit of the line with that SKU. Optional parts appear in the order shown. RATE is what core.ParseRate accepts, at most 100%; QTY, BUY and FREE are positive integers written only with digits; AMOUNT is what core.ParseMoney accepts, above zero. With a cap, a rule takes at most AMOUNT off a line. Rates apply with Money.MulRate. Any other line returns a nil slice and an *Error whose Line is the 1-based line number; Msg is free text. (r Rule) String() formats a parsed rule as ParseRules reads it, on one line with single spaces: rates by Rate.String, amounts by Money.String, counts in decimal, tiers as QTY:RATE, min only when above 1 and cap only when set, so a rule's String parses back to a rule with the same String. Line(item core.LineItem, rules []Rule) core.Money applies the one rule in rules that takes the most off item: rules never combine, and when none applies nothing is taken off.

list.domain: rules texts of 0-5 percent, tier, bundle and off lines over a few categories and SKUs, with blank, comment and padded lines; half the texts also draw invalid rates, amounts, counts, tiers and keywords; each applied to four single-line invoices of 1-12 units at up to 200.00

list.checks: ParseTable values and error lines, Table.String, and Rate and Line for exempt SKUs, categories, thresholds and the default

requirement.text: ParseTable(text string) (Table, error) reads a tax table, one entry per line, with discount.ParseRules's line rules (split at \n; trim spaces, tabs and \r; skip blank lines and lines starting with #; fields separated by whitespace). The entries are rate CATEGORY RATE [over AMOUNT RATE2], where lines in CATEGORY whose Unit is above AMOUNT pay RATE2 instead of RATE; default RATE, the rate of categories without a rate entry; and exempt SKU, a SKU that pays no tax. RATE and RATE2 are what core.ParseRate accepts, and AMOUNT is what core.ParseMoney accepts, not negative. A category, the default or an exempt SKU given twice, or any other line, returns a zero Table and an *Error whose Line is the 1-based line number. The zero Table taxes nothing. (t Table) Rate(item core.LineItem) core.Rate returns 0 for an exempt SKU, otherwise the rate of item's category (RATE2 when its Unit is above AMOUNT), otherwise the default rate, otherwise 0. (t Table) Line(item core.LineItem, net core.Money) core.Money returns the tax on item when its price after discount is net: net.MulRate(t.Rate(item)), so tax is rounded per line. (t Table) String() formats t as ParseTable reads it: the default entry if there is one, then the rate entries sorted by category, then the exempt entries sorted by SKU, one per line with single spaces, each ending in \n, rates by Rate.String and amounts by Money.String.

list.domain: tax tables with a default half the time, rates for about half the categories (some over a threshold) and some exempt SKUs; half the tables are 0-5 entries that may be invalid or repeated; each rated on four lines priced at or around the thresholds, with nets up to 500.00
excluded: error messages
whitespace other than ASCII space and tab

list.checks: ParseTable values and error lines, Table.String, and Convert's route, tie-break, rounding and whole currencies

requirement.text: ParseTable(text string) (Table, error) reads exchange rates, one entry per line, with discount.ParseRules's line rules. FROM TO RATE means one unit of FROM is worth RATE units of TO: FROM and TO are different codes of three ASCII capital letters, and RATE is what core.ParseRate accepts, above zero and without %. A pair may be given once, in either direction. whole CODE marks a currency without minor units, once per code. Any other line returns a zero Table and an *Error whose Line is the 1-based line number. (t Table) Convert(m core.Money, from, to string) (core.Money, error) returns m unchanged when from equals to. Otherwise it converts along the route of fewest pairs, and among equally short routes the one whose sequence of currencies is alphabetically first, compared currency by currency. A step along a pair as given is m.MulRate(RATE), a step against it is core.DivRound(m × 1,000,000, RATE), and a step into a whole currency then rounds to whole units, a multiple of 100 cents, halves away from zero. With no route it returns an error. (t Table) String() formats t as ParseTable reads it: the whole entries sorted by code, then the pairs as given sorted by FROM and then TO, one per line with single spaces, each ending in \n, rates as decimals without trailing zeros or a trailing .

list.domain: exchange tables pairing each two of USD, EUR, JPY, GBP and CHF half the time in either direction, rates 0.25 to 4, each currency whole one time in five; half the tables are 0-5 lines that may be invalid or repeated; four conversions each of up to ±10,000.00 between those codes, usd and the same code

list.checks: the whole table text: widths, alignment, Max, multi-line cells, missing and extra cells, rules and footer

requirement.text: Table(cols []Column, rows, footer [][]string) string lays out a plain-text table, with Column{Title string; Right bool; Max int}. With no columns it returns "". The title line comes first, then a rule, then the rows; when footer is nonempty, another rule and then the footer rows follow. A row's missing cells are empty, and cells beyond the columns are ignored. A cell's text is split at \n into cell lines, and a row prints as many lines as its tallest cell, at least one. When Max > 0, a cell line, titles included, longer than Max runes is cut to its first Max − 1 runes followed by …. Each column is as wide as its widest cell line, in runes. Each printed line pads every cell line with spaces to its column's width, on the left when Right is set and on the right otherwise, joins them with two spaces and drops trailing spaces; a rule is each column's width in -, joined the same way. Every line ends in \n.

list.checks: Format over int64, its extremes included, Parse's values and ErrInvalidAmount on near and malformed amounts, and Parse of Format

requirement.text: Package `money` (bottom layer). Provides `type Cents int64` (an amount in hundredths of the currency unit), `func Format(c Cents) string`, `func Parse(s string) (Cents, error)` and `var ErrInvalidAmount` (message `invalid amount`). Format writes a leading `-` for negative amounts, then the whole units with no leading zeros (`0` when under one unit) and no thousands separators, then `.` and exactly two digits. Examples: 0 gives `0.00`, 5 gives `0.05`, 1250 gives `12.50`, -75 gives `-0.75`, 123456789 gives `1234567.89`. It must be correct across the whole int64 range, including the minimum value (`-92233720368547758.08`). Parse accepts an optional leading `-`, then one or more ASCII digits, then optionally a `.` followed by one or two digits, and nothing else: no spaces, no `+`, no separators. Examples: `12` gives 1200, `12.5` gives 1250, `007.05` gives 705, `-3.10` gives -310, `-0` gives 0. Inputs such as the empty string, `-`, `.5`, `12.`, `12.345`, `+1`, ` 1` and `1,000`, and any value outside the int64 range, return 0 and `ErrInvalidAmount` itself.

list.domain: any int64, its extremes and amounts up to ±1000.00; amounts as an optional -, 1-20 digits and an optional . with 0-3 digits, strings of 0-7 characters from digits, '-', '.', '+', ' ' and ',', and edge strings at the int64 limits

list.checks: Parse's values and ErrInvalidDate, and String, AddDays, Weekday and DaysBetween (both ends counted, as corrected) on valid dates

requirement.text: Package `calendar` (bottom layer). Provides `type Date struct { Year, Month, Day int }` (Month is 1 to 12), `func Parse(s string) (Date, error)`, `func (d Date) String() string`, `func (d Date) AddDays(n int) Date`, `func (d Date) Weekday() time.Weekday`, `func DaysBetween(from, to Date) int` and `var ErrInvalidDate` (message `invalid date`). Parse accepts exactly the form `YYYY-MM-DD`: ten characters, ASCII digits, with `-` at the 5th and 8th positions. The year must be 1900 to 2999, and the date must exist in the Gregorian calendar. A leap year is divisible by 4, except century years not divisible by 400. `2024-02-29` parses. `2026-02-29`, `2026-13-01`, `2026-1-05`, `2026-01-05 ` (trailing space) and `1899-12-31` each return the zero Date and `ErrInvalidDate` itself. String renders a date as `YYYY-MM-DD` with zero padding, for example `2026-03-07`. AddDays moves forward (positive n) or backward (negative n) by n calendar days, crossing month and year boundaries: 2026-12-31 plus 1 is 2027-01-01, and 2024-03-01 minus 1 is 2024-02-29. The result is not range-checked. Weekday gives the day of the week; 2026-11-09 is a Monday. DaysBetween returns the number of days from `from` to `to`, negative when `to` is earlier: 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-30 is 21, the reverse is -21, and a date to itself is 0. Inputs to AddDays, Weekday and DaysBetween are assumed to be valid dates; behaviour for invalid ones is unspecified.

list.domain: strings in the YYYY-MM-DD shape with years 1890-3010, months 0-13 and days 0-32, valid dates and edge strings; valid dates in years 1900-2999, mostly 2025-2028, moved by -2000 to 2000 days
excluded: AddDays, Weekday and DaysBetween on invalid dates

list.checks: ParseKind's values and ErrUnknownKind on spellings near the three names, and String on any Kind

requirement.text: Package `item` (bottom layer). Provides `type Kind int` with constants `Book` (1), `DVD` (2) and `Magazine` (3), `func ParseKind(s string) (Kind, error)`, `func (k Kind) String() string` and `var ErrUnknownKind` (message `unknown item kind`). The zero Kind, and any value other than 1 to 3, is not a valid kind. ParseKind ignores leading and trailing spaces and tabs. It matches `book`, `dvd` or `magazine` regardless of ASCII letter case, so `Book`, ` DVD ` and `MAGAZINE` all parse. Anything else, including the empty string and `books`, returns 0 and `ErrUnknownKind` itself. String returns `book`, `dvd` or `magazine` for the three kinds and `unknown` for any other value.

list.domain: the three names and near misses, letters upper-cased at random, padded with spaces, tabs, a line feed or a carriage return; kinds -2 to 5

list.checks: DueDate's date, the Sunday rule included, and ErrInvalidKind

requirement.text: Package `loan` (middle layer). Provides `func DueDate(kind item.Kind, checkout calendar.Date) (calendar.Date, error)`. The loan period is 21 days for a book, 7 days for a DVD and 14 days for a magazine. The due date is the checkout date plus the loan period. The library is closed on Sundays, so a due date that falls on a Sunday moves to the following Monday. Examples: a book checked out 2026-11-09 is due 2026-11-30. A DVD checked out on Sunday 2026-11-08 is due 2026-11-16, because 2026-11-15 is a Sunday. A magazine checked out 2026-11-01 is due 2026-11-16. A kind other than Book, DVD or Magazine returns the zero Date and `loan.ErrInvalidKind` itself (message `invalid item kind`).

list.domain: valid kinds five times in six, else 0, 4, -1 or 9; valid checkout dates as L2 draws them

list.checks: LateFee's fee, its caps and ErrInvalidKind

requirement.text: Package `loan` (middle layer). Provides `func LateFee(kind item.Kind, due, returned calendar.Date) (money.Cents, error)`. An item returned on or before its due date owes no fee. Otherwise the fee is the number of days late (calendar days from the due date to the return date) times the daily rate, capped at a maximum for each kind. A book costs 25 cents a day, up to 1000. A DVD costs 100 a day, up to 2000. A magazine costs 10 a day, up to 300. Examples: a book due 2026-11-30 and returned 2026-12-03 owes 75. A DVD due 2026-10-01 and returned 2026-11-09 (39 days late) owes 2000. A magazine returned one day late owes 10. Anything returned on or before its due date owes 0. A kind other than Book, DVD or Magazine returns 0 and `loan.ErrInvalidKind` itself, whatever the dates.

list.domain: kinds as L4 draws them; valid due dates; returns from 10 days early to 90 days late

list.checks: Renew's new due date and the first sentinel in its check order

requirement.text: Package `loan` (middle layer). Provides `func Renew(kind item.Kind, due, today calendar.Date, renewals int) (calendar.Date, error)`, where `renewals` is how many times the loan has already been renewed. Checks are made in the following order, and the first failure is returned as the sentinel itself, together with the zero Date. (1) A kind other than Book, DVD or Magazine gives `ErrInvalidKind`. (2) A negative renewals count gives `ErrInvalidRenewals` (message `invalid renewal count`). (3) A today later than due gives `ErrOverdue` (message `loan is overdue`). (4) A renewals count already at the maximum for the kind gives `ErrRenewalLimit` (message `renewal limit reached`). The maximum is 2 for a book, 1 for a DVD and 0 for a magazine. Renewing on the due date itself is allowed. On success, the new due date is the current due date plus the kind's loan period (book 21 days, DVD 7, magazine 14), moved to the following Monday if it falls on a Sunday. The new due date counts from the current due date, not from today. Examples: a book due 2026-11-30, renewed on 2026-11-20 with 0 prior renewals, is now due 2026-12-21. The same book with 2 prior renewals gives `ErrRenewalLimit`. A DVD due 2026-11-16 renewed on 2026-11-17 gives `ErrOverdue`. A magazine renewed on or before its due date gives `ErrRenewalLimit`.

list.domain: kinds as L4 draws them; valid due dates; today from 6 days before to 4 days after; renewal counts -1 to 3

list.checks: CanBorrow's sentinel in its check order

requirement.text: Package `loan` (middle layer). Provides `type Category int` with constants `Adult` (1) and `Child` (2), and `func CanBorrow(cat Category, current []item.Kind, next item.Kind) error`. It says whether a member who already holds the items in `current` may borrow one more item of kind `next`. An adult may hold 10 items in total, of which at most 3 may be DVDs. A child may hold 5 items in total, of which at most 1 may be a DVD. Books and magazines count only toward the total. Checks are made in the following order, and the first failure is returned as the sentinel itself. (1) A category other than Adult or Child gives `ErrInvalidCategory` (message `invalid member category`). (2) A `next`, or any element of `current`, that is not a valid kind gives `ErrInvalidKind`. (3) If holding `current` plus `next` would exceed the total limit, it gives `ErrTotalLimit` (message `total loan limit reached`). (4) If `next` is a DVD and the DVDs in `current` plus this one would exceed the DVD limit, it gives `ErrKindLimit` (message `dvd loan limit reached`). Otherwise it returns nil. A nil or empty `current` means nothing is held. Examples: an adult holding 9 books may borrow a 10th item but not an 11th. An adult holding 3 DVDs may borrow a book but not a DVD. A child holding 1 DVD and 4 books gets `ErrTotalLimit` when asking for a further DVD.

list.domain: categories Adult and Child seven times in eight, else 0, 3 or -1; nil holdings one time in ten, else 0-12 valid kinds with an occasional invalid one; next a valid kind nine times in ten

list.checks: ParseLoan's values, errors.Is ErrMalformedLine and its error message

requirement.text: Package `report` (top layer). Provides `type Loan struct { ItemID string; Kind item.Kind; Checkout calendar.Date; Returned calendar.Date; IsReturned bool }`, `func ParseLoan(line string) (Loan, error)` and `var ErrMalformedLine` (message `malformed loan line`). A loan line has four comma-separated fields: item ID, kind, checkout date and return date. Examples are `BK-0042,book,2026-10-01,` and `DVD-0001,dvd,2026-10-19,2026-10-25`. Before parsing, one trailing line feed is removed if present, and then one trailing carriage return is removed if present. There is no quoting or escaping. Leading and trailing spaces and tabs are removed from each field. The item ID must be 1 to 20 characters long, each an uppercase ASCII letter, an ASCII digit or `-`. The kind must be `book`, `dvd` or `magazine`, in any ASCII letter case. The checkout date, and the return date when present, use the form `YYYY-MM-DD` with a real Gregorian date in years 1900 to 2999. An empty return field means the item is still out: `IsReturned` is false and `Returned` is the zero Date. A return date earlier than the checkout date is an error; a return on the checkout date is fine. Validation stops at the first problem, checked in the following order, and the error message names the problem. (1) A wrong number of fields gives `malformed loan line: field count`. (2) A bad item ID gives `malformed loan line: item id`. (3) A bad kind gives `malformed loan line: kind`. (4) A bad checkout date gives `malformed loan line: checkout`. (5) A bad return date gives `malformed loan line: returned`. (6) A return before checkout gives `malformed loan line: returned before checkout`. Every error is returned with the zero Loan and satisfies `errors.Is(err, report.ErrMalformedLine)`.

list.checks: OverdueReport's text and errors.Is ErrInvalidKind

requirement.text: Package `report` (top layer). Provides `func OverdueReport(loans []Loan, today calendar.Date) (string, error)`. A loan is overdue when it has not been returned and `today` is strictly later than its due date. The due date is the checkout date plus 21 days for a book, 7 for a DVD or 14 for a magazine, moved to the following Monday if it falls on a Sunday. Days overdue is the number of calendar days from the due date to today. The fee is days overdue times the daily rate, capped: a book costs 0.25 a day up to 10.00, a DVD 1.00 a day up to 20.00, and a magazine 0.10 a day up to 3.00. Returned loans are ignored entirely. The report is plain text. Every line, including the last, ends with a single line feed. Fields within a line are separated by a single tab character. The first line is `Overdue loans as of ` followed by today in the form YYYY-MM-DD. Next comes one line per overdue loan, with five fields: the item ID; the kind (`book`, `dvd` or `magazine`); the due date as YYYY-MM-DD; the days overdue, written `1 day` or `N days`; and the fee, written with exactly two decimal places and no currency symbol. Lines are ordered by days overdue, most first. Ties are ordered by item ID in ascending byte order, and any remaining ties keep their input order. Duplicate item IDs are all listed. The last line is `Total: `, then the count written as `1 item` or `N items` (`0 items` when there are none), then a comma and a space, then the sum of the listed fees in the same two-decimal form. Example: today is 2026-11-09, and three loans are unreturned. `DVD-0001` is a dvd checked out 2026-10-19. `BK-0042` is a book checked out 2026-10-01. `MAG-7` is a magazine checked out 2026-10-26, which is due today and so is not overdue. The report is these four lines: `Overdue loans as of 2026-11-09`, then `BK-0042<TAB>book<TAB>2026-10-22<TAB>18 days<TAB>4.50`, then `DVD-0001<TAB>dvd<TAB>2026-10-26<TAB>14 days<TAB>14.00`, then `Total: 2 items, 18.50`. With nothing overdue, the report is the two lines `Overdue loans as of 2026-11-09` and `Total: 0 items, 0.00`. If an unreturned loan has a kind other than book, dvd or magazine, the function returns the empty string and an error satisfying `errors.Is(err, loan.ErrInvalidKind)`.

list.domain: 0-6 loans from five IDs, repeated, valid kinds with an occasional invalid one, checkouts up to 60 days before today, often shared with the previous loan, a quarter returned

judge.runtime: the run configuration's runtime_version, runtime_sha256 and model (evaluation/config.json)
judge.session: No tools and a fresh session per call. (#228 decision 15)
judge.value: The median of the k calls per dimension; the spread is shown. (#228 decision 18)
judge.retry: A failed or unparseable call is retried once. If any rating is still missing, the run's judge value is missing. (#228 decision 18)
judge.material: The requirement text, verbatim, the formatted initial code and the formatted change. File names are removed from the code; Rust inline test modules are moved out; all test code is shown as one block. The reference is not shown. (#228 decision 16; amended in version 4)

maintainability.1: Control flow is needlessly convoluted or hard to follow; names mislead; a reader must trace the code by hand to see what it does.
maintainability.3: Readable with effort: some needless indirection, nesting or unclear names, but the intent can be recovered.
maintainability.5: Straightforward: each function does one clear thing, names say what values are, and control flow is as direct as the task allows.

duplication.1: Logic is copied rather than shared: the same rule is written out in two or more places, so a fix would have to be made twice.
duplication.3: Some repeated logic that could reasonably have been shared, but each rule is mostly written once.
duplication.5: Each rule is written once and reused where it is needed; no copied-in logic.

unnecessary_changes.1: The change rewrites or reshapes code the requirements did not ask to change, or adds behaviour nobody asked for.
unnecessary_changes.3: Mostly on task, with some edits to code the requirements did not touch.
unnecessary_changes.5: Every edit serves a requirement; untouched code is left as it was.

test_quality.1: Tests cover only the happy path, or assert little; the edge cases the requirements name are untested.
test_quality.3: Tests cover the main behaviour and some named edge cases, but miss others.
test_quality.5: Tests are focused and cover the behaviour and the edge cases the requirements name, with clear assertions.

blinding.question: This change was written by two AI agents working on the same task. Which is more likely? Answer with exactly one letter. A: they worked in separate Git worktrees, and their work was then merged. B: they worked in one shared workspace.
blinding.calls: A separate fresh call per final snapshot, on the same material. Each fixture's judge cells print `arm guessed k/n`, with no label and no cutoff. (#228 decision 19)
blinding.team_of_one: Not asked: the question assumes two agents. A one-agent run is rated but makes no blinding call. (#336)
blinding.note: Chance is about n/2. A count far from n/2 in either direction means the arm can be guessed from the material, so treat the judge ratings for this fixture as possibly unblinded.

judge.known_answer_set: Per fixture, the known-answer base: the formatted reference plus one test file covering the behaviour and the edge cases the requirements name, since the reference has no tests. Then four degraded copies of that base, one per dimension: copied-in logic (duplication), an untouched function rewritten or behaviour nobody asked for (unnecessary_changes), happy-path-only tests (test_quality), needlessly convoluted control flow (maintainability). The base and copies are in protected/known-answer.json; `known-answer` checks them. (#228 decision 20, amended by #233)
judge.calibration_record: `known-answer --judge CONFIG` rates the base and each copy k times and writes calibration/v{version}.json, named by this file's version and recording the manifest version. A record is never overwritten. (#233) With --fixtures it rates only fixtures in uncalibrated_fixtures, whose judged inputs changed; the other fixtures keep their record. (#263)
judge.subtlety_rule: Each copy changes one declaration, changed or added, aimed at one dimension. It passes the oracle, all properties, vet and clippy with no findings on changed lines, and the formatter. No comment names or hints at the defect. It must be code a competent agent could write under the 30-minute limit. Daniel signs off each copy as plausible before it freezes. (#228 decision 21)
judge.calibration_criterion: On every fixture, the targeted copy's median over three calls is lower than the reference's on that dimension. The #27 runs are rated for information only. (#228 decision 22)
judge.amendment_rule: A failing dimension gets at most one versioned amendment to its prompt and anchors, checked against the same frozen copies, before any scored code is opened. The copies are never changed after the first calibration call. A dimension that fails twice is dropped. (#228 decision 23)

wording.flat: No difference detected at the sensitivity of the known-answer set: per fixture, the reference and one oracle-passing copy per dimension, each changing one declaration

missing.tool_failures: A formatter error, a crashing tool or a suite that does not compile makes that metric missing for that run, with the tool's error as the reason. It is never retried, never imputed and never counted as a quality failure. (#228 decision 25)
missing.versions: Each run's metrics record go version, rustc -V, clippy-driver -V and rustfmt -V. The pins are rust-toolchain.toml and the evaluation's recorded Go version. (#228 decision 26)

rules.lasts: Until #228's stage 2 freezes. Lifted by #233: stage 2 is frozen with the calibration record calibration/v2.json, so a scored run's final code may be inspected. Lifted for go-relationships by #263, recalibrated on fixture 3 version 2 (calibration/v4.json).
rules.inspection: Nobody opens a scored run's final tree, diffs, transcripts, events.jsonl or session JSONL, and nobody runs report --show-code on a scored batch. (#228 decision 30)
rules.diagnosis: A session diagnosing an infrastructure or safety failure may open any file in the failed run's own directory, plus code-free batch files. It must not open other runs' directories. The ticket comment lists the run and every file opened. A failed run is never measured, and its replacement runs in a new directory. (#228 decision 31)
rules.batch_checkout: Every invocation of the scored batch, including resumes and shards, runs from a checkout of #188's freeze commit. (#228 decision 29a)
